analysis.one_liner: Narrows when a franchisor or client company counts as the employer of franchise and temp workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced May 13, 2021 with 13 of 50 Senate Republicans cosponsoring, it sat in the Senate labor committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the definition of a "joint employer" in two core labor laws. A company would count as the employer of another company's workers only if it directly controls the essentials — hiring, firing, pay, benefits, day-to-day supervision, scheduling, and discipline. That would stop the federal labor board and courts from treating fast-food franchisors, staffing-agency clients, and lead contractors as employers of the people actually doing the work, freeing them from union bargaining duties and wage liability.
analysis.who_benefits: Franchise corporations, staffing agencies, and lead contractors are the main beneficiaries. Under the bill, they would no longer be treated as employers of people hired by franchisees or temp agencies unless they directly control the essentials of the job, so they could not be forced to bargain with unions or held liable for unpaid wages at franchised and outsourced worksites [S2, S3]. Small-business franchisees also gain relief from joint liability and from being drawn into labor disputes involving the national brand [S3].

how_it_helps.text: A company would be a joint employer only if it directly, actually, and immediately exercises significant control over the essential terms of employment — hiring, firing, pay and benefits, day-to-day supervision, scheduling, and discipline — under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Under the labor law, that would keep unions and workers from naming the franchisor or lead company as their employer in organizing and unfair-labor-practice cases at franchised or outsourced worksites, since indirect control would no longer count.

Under the wage law, brands and corporate clients would not owe minimum wage or overtime when a franchisee or staffing agency underpays workers, and workers could not pursue the deep-pocketed company for the unpaid wages.

Because the change would be written into federal statute, it would permanently insulate franchised and outsourced arrangements from the labor board decisions that had broadened the joint-employer standard.

analysis.who_pays: Workers at franchised and outsourced workplaces — fast-food counters, hotel staff, temp warehouse crews, janitors — would lose the ability to bargain with, or recover unpaid wages from, the big company that profits from their work; only the franchisee or agency employing them on paper would be responsible. Unions would lose one of their main routes into franchised and subcontracted workplaces.

drawbacks.text: Workers could bargain and file claims only against the franchisee or staffing agency, even where the brand effectively sets the economics — required prices, suppliers, and fees — that shape those workers' pay.
If the franchisee or agency shuts down, unpaid wages and other violations would be far harder to collect, since the big company would no longer be jointly responsible.

The bill would lock the narrow standard into statute, ending the back-and-forth in which the labor board broadened joint-employer coverage under Democratic administrations and narrowed it under Republican ones — an approach unions saw as stripping a key protection.

Supporters' good-faith case: the existing broad standard treated franchisors as employers of workers they never hired or supervised and dragged local businesses into disputes with national brands; the bill restores a direct-control test consistent with its 'Save Local Business' name.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine argument for a clearer, control-based test: legal standards flipped with each labor board appointee, and franchisors with no real role in employment faced employer duties. But this bill goes further — it relieves the companies that set franchise and outsourcing economics of any wage or bargaining responsibility toward the people doing the work, shifting that burden onto workers and thin intermediaries. The gains in legal certainty come chiefly at workers' expense.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 13, 2021, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed; the action record after the referral is empty.
It died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023, without either chamber ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, workers at franchised and outsourced workplaces kept the joint-employer rights that existed under then-current law; franchise brands and staffing firms failed to get the statutory liability shield they sought.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 13, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the HELP Committee.

for.name: 13 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Sens. Scott of South Carolina, Inhofe, Burr, Cassidy, and Braun.

for.name: Franchise and restaurant industry groups
for.what_they_did: Long lobbied for a narrow joint-employer standard of the kind this bill writes into law, to keep brands out of franchisee workers' union disputes and wage claims.

against.name: Sen. Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it received no committee action after its May 2021 referral.

against.name: Labor unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed narrowing the joint-employer standard, which lets fast-food and outsourced workers bargain with and bring claims against national brands.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — 13 of 50 Senate Republicans joined Sen. Marshall — and the Democratic-run labor committee gave the bill no action.

industries.industry: Franchise corporations (fast-food, hotel, and retail brands)
industries.note: The bill would make a franchisor the employer of franchise workers only if it directly controls hiring, pay, supervision, scheduling, and discipline, freeing it of bargaining duties and wage liability for those workers. Brands would keep collecting royalties and dictating prices and suppliers without the legal duties of an employer.

Corporate clients could hire through temp agencies and subcontractors without sharing responsibility for minimum wage, overtime, or union rights, making outsourcing cheaper and more common. Workers could pursue only the thin intermediary, not the profitable company at the top.

The broad joint-employer standard is one of unions' main tools for organizing franchised fast-food and outsourced workplaces; narrowing it removes the path of bargaining with or charging the national brand. This runs against workers' interests too.

They would be freed from joint liability and from brand entanglement in labor disputes, which is the bill's pitched benefit. But they would remain the sole employer — the only target for workers' wage claims and union efforts — while the brand sheds responsibility.
